stories.title: Sugon 8000 Breaks Kilometer-Scale Global Weather Forecasting Bottleneck with Domestic Compute Power
China vows to curb tech bubbles, keep AI risks in check
stories.summary: The guidelines warned against blind investment and excessive expansion into emerging sectors
stories.content:
The guidelines warned against blind investment and excessive expansion into emerging sectors

[BEIJING] China will tighten oversight of its drive into advanced technology, seeking to curb investment bubbles while ensuring artificial intelligence remains “safe, reliable and controllable”, according to policy guidelines issued on Friday (Oct 9).

As Beijing ramps up support for high-tech manufacturing and strategic industries to boost technological self-sufficiency amid rivalry with the US, the guidelines warned against blind investment and excessive expansion into emerging sectors.

“Developing new productive forces is an inherent requirement and an important focus for promoting high-quality development,” Xinhua cited the guidelines, issued by the ruling Communist Party and the cabinet, as saying.

President Xi Jinping introduced the term “new productive forces” in 2023, emphasising scientific research, technological breakthroughs and industrial upgrading across China’s manufacturing base.

The guidelines said China would seek breakthroughs in AI theory and core technologies, strengthen the supply of computing power, algorithms and data, and establish national pilot bases for industrial AI applications. They also called for technology monitoring, risk-warning and emergency-response systems to ensure AI remains “safe, reliable and controllable”.

China will fully implement its “AI Plus” initiative, using AI to upgrade traditional industries and accelerate the rollout of intelligent products including connected new-energy vehicles, AI-enabled phones and computers, and humanoid robots, the document said.

The guidelines also pledged to strengthen “original and disruptive” innovation in core technologies and to use China’s state-led “new nationwide system” to speed the development and deployment of landmark products.

At the same time, officials were told to prioritise the real economy and avoid bubbles, industrial hollowing-out, blind investment and “swarm-like” rushes into high-tech sectors.

China will “strictly prohibit the illegal or improper abuse of policies in the name of developing new productive forces,” the guidelines said, adding that officials responsible for major losses caused by blind investment would be held accountable.

The document also called for the healthy and orderly development of the low-altitude economy — businesses built around civilian drones, air taxis, small aircraft and related services — while ensuring safety. REUTERS

stories.title: Digital Realty begins work on KIX15 data center in Japan
stories.summary: Digital Realty has commenced construction of its KIX15 facility in the Osaka area, adding to its footprint in Japan's second-largest data center market. The project expands the REIT's KIX campus, which serves cloud and enterprise customers seeking capacity outside the crowded Tokyo metro.
stories.why_it_matters: The build reflects growing hyperscaler demand for capacity in Osaka as a geographic complement to Tokyo, and it reinforces Japan's position as one of Asia's most actively developed data center markets, with implications for land, power, and contractor availability in the Kansai region.
stories.content:
Digital Realty has begun construction work on a data center at its Osaka campus in Japan.

Dubbed KIX15, the building will add 24MW of capacity to the KIX Campus located in Ibaraki City, Osaka Prefecture.

KIX15 is being developed through the MC Digital Realty (MCDR) joint venture, a 50/50 joint venture with Mitsubishi Corporation, and will be the fifth building at the campus.

Operations are expected to begin in Q4 2028. The new data center will bring the MCDR's total capacity in Japan to 220MW of IT capacity.

Serene Nah, managing director and head of Asia Pacific, Digital Realty, said: “Japan is a strategic market for Digital Realty and a key part of our long-term growth in Asia Pacific. Our continued investment in Japan reflects both our confidence in the market and our commitment to building the infrastructure customers will need for the long term.

“KIX15 is the next step in that commitment. As customer requirements become more distributed and complex, the combination of local scale and global reach will become increasingly important.”

Kohei Yamashita, representative director and CEO of MC Digital Realty, added: “Kansai has a growing opportunity to play a larger role in Japan’s AI economy. Realizing that potential will require an ecosystem that can support businesses as they build and scale AI, bringing together computing infrastructure, connectivity, and technology expertise.”

The data center will be designed to support hybrid air- and liquid-cooling technologies.

Earlier this year, Digital Realty added a third data center to its NRT campus in Inzai City, Japan, located approximately 71km (44 miles) from downtown Tokyo. Work on the 31MW NRT14 began in May 2024.

The company also has a fourth data center in the Tokyo region, dubbed HND10.

stories.title: Report: Nvidia plans to invest in inference chip startup d-Matrix
stories.content:
Nvidia is planning to invest in inference chip startup d-Matrix, according to a report from The Information.

Citing three people with knowledge of the deal, the report said the planned investment is part of an effort by Nvidia to make its technology compatible with rival chip designs.

The report comes a month after d-Matrix announced it would adopt Nvidia’s NVLink technology to connect its Raptor processors with the chip giant’s hardware in rack-scale solutions. First unveiled in May 2025 and known as NVLink Fusion, the interconnect technology allows partners to build semi-custom AI infrastructure linking non-Nvidia accelerators with Nvidia hardware.

Other NVLink Fusion partners include the likes of Arm, Fujitsu, Intel, MediaTek, Qualcomm, SiFive, and Synopsys.

Founded in 2019 and headquartered in Santa Clara, d-Matrix develops accelerator cards that aim to make AI inferencing workloads quicker and more efficient. Its full-stack platform is powered by the company’s Corsair inference accelerators, JetStream NICS, and Aviator software, which it claims can deliver 10X faster performance, 3X lower cost, and 3–5X better energy efficiency than GPU-based systems.

In November 2025, the startup closed a $275 million Series C funding round, valuing the company at $2 billion. The Information separately reported in July 2026 that d-Matrix was looking to raise additional financing, targeting a $5bn valuation.

stories.title: Bitdeer AI signs 67MW AI cloud agreement in Malaysia
stories.summary: Bitdeer AI has signed an agreement covering 67MW of AI cloud capacity in Malaysia, committing the Singapore-headquartered firm to a significant deployment in the country. The deal extends Bitdeer's push beyond crypto mining into AI compute services, where it has been repurposing infrastructure and capital toward GPU cloud offerings.
stories.why_it_matters: The 67MW commitment adds to Malaysia's growing tally of AI-oriented capacity deals and illustrates how former crypto-mining operators are converting their power access and data center assets into AI infrastructure, intensifying competition for electricity allocations in key Malaysian markets.
stories.content:
Neocloud Bitdeer AI has entered into a 10-year data center services agreement in Malaysia.

The company will lease the A901 data center in Malaysia, a 67MW campus in Malaysia. The exact location and operator of the data center have not been provided.

A901 will be Bitdeer's third location in Malaysia, joining its data centers in Cyberjaya and Johor, and bringing its global contracted capacity across Malaysia, Norway, and the US to 273.5MW, 78 percent of its goal of 350MW by Q1 2028.

Capacity at A901 is expected to start being delivered in Q1 of 2027, completing in Q2. The site will be engineered for liquid-cooled Nvidia GB300 NVL72 systems.

“Demand for liquid-cooled, rack-scale AI capacity in Southeast Asia is running ahead of what the market can deliver, and customers are asking for it earlier and in larger blocks,” said Michael G. Potter, chief financial officer of Bitdeer Technologies Group. “A901 adds 67MW in a third Malaysian location, which widens the set of sites and delivery dates we can put in front of a customer."

The lease comes just weeks after Bitdeer AI signed another agreement for A202, a 65.1MW data center facility in Johor Bahru.

Bitdeer started as a cryptominer, but it has increasingly pivoted to data centers and cloud services. The firm is repurposing mining facilities in Washington, Tennessee, and Norway into AI hosting.

The company also recently signed a non-binding letter of intent to develop an AI data center in Bhutan's Gelephu Mindfulness City, targeting an initial 30MW of renewable hydro/solar-powered capacity with a potential expansion pathway to 500MW.

stories.title: Wes Maas made a big bet on Firmus. Now his company is paying the price
stories.summary: Wes Maas's decision to build a major position in Firmus through Maas Group is now weighing on his company following the neocloud's scrapped IPO. What was framed as a transformative bet on AI infrastructure has instead exposed the construction group to valuation and liquidity risk tied to a single private asset.
stories.why_it_matters: The episode highlights the governance and concentration risks of listed companies taking outsized venture-style positions in unlisted AI infrastructure firms, and it may make boards and investors more cautious about similar cross-holdings in the sector.
stories.content:
Maas has moved to assuage shareholder fears about its exposure to artificial intelligence infrastructure company Firmus Technologies after the latter pulled its proposed $44 billion float because of a lack of investor interest.

Maas, founded by former rugby league footballer Wes Maas, owns a 3.2 per cent stake in Firmus, and has $1.1 billion in contracts for electrical engineering work required for Firmus’ planned data centre network across Australia.

stories.title: Firmus float failure turns to blame game, with brokers at the centre
stories.summary: In the aftermath of Firmus's failed IPO, recriminations have begun over who bears responsibility, with the brokers who ran the bookbuild at the center of the dispute. Questions are being raised about pricing expectations, deal timing, and how demand was gauged before the float was pulled.
stories.why_it_matters: The blame game could reshape how future AI infrastructure listings are marketed in Australia, with issuers and underwriters likely to demand more conservative pricing and longer anchor books, potentially slowing the pipeline of data center and compute companies seeking public capital.
stories.content:
Major Firmus Technologies investors have accused the heavyweight investment banking syndicate working on the unsuccessful $44 billion listing of providing misleading information and leaving them in the dark as recriminations over who was at fault for the failure begin to grow.

After two days of discussions, Firmus pulled plans to raise $US5.5 billion ($7.9 billion) and list on the ASX in what would have been the biggest initial public offering since Telstra three decades ago. Instead, the Nvidia-backed company is working on plans to pursue a listing on the Nasdaq.

stories.title: The fundies who cashed in on Firmus before the IPO dream fizzled
stories.content:
Firmus Technologies’ blockbuster float might be dead in the water, but its meteoric rise in the past year has already beefed up returns for a select group of funds in what has otherwise been a tough time for active managers on the Australian sharemarket.

The artificial intelligence infrastructure firm pulled its IPO on Friday morning after bankers working on the proposed $44 billion listing veered from discussing the need to rework the float and cutting its valuation, to cancelling the float altogether.

stories.title: Asia data centre boom vulnerable to US policies, Jardine says
stories.summary: The head of Jardine Matheson has warned that Asia's data center investment boom is politically fragile because much of it depends on a small number of US technology giants whose global operations could be disrupted by Washington's shifting posture toward China. Billions of dollars of committed capital across the region ride on decisions those hyperscalers may be forced to make.
stories.why_it_matters: The warning reframes Asia's data center pipeline as a concentration-risk story: developers, lenders, and governments from Singapore to Malaysia could see demand evaporate if US-China tensions restrict American hyperscalers' regional expansion, making geopolitical exposure a core underwriting consideration.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Oct 9): Asia’s booming data-centre industry faces growing political risks as billions of dollars in investment hinge on a handful of US technology giants whose ability to operate globally could be upended by Washington’s increasingly unpredictable stance toward China, according to the chief of one of Hong Kong’s biggest conglomerates.

“The risk we think the most about at this point is actually political risk,” Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd chief executive officer Lincoln Pan told the Milken Asia Summit in Singapore on Friday. “If you look at this debate about the US and China and the significant bets many people are making around this sector, particularly around data centres and AI large language models coming out of the US, it’s a highly concentrated bet on the stability of US data policy.”

Private equity giants including Blackstone Inc and KKR & Co have poured billions of dollars into Asian data centres, betting that the explosive growth of artificial intelligence and cloud computing will fuel demand for computing capacity for years to come.

While Asia’s digital infrastructure will struggle to keep pace with that demand, those facilities depend heavily on US hyperscalers that operate and are influenced significantly by US government policy, said Pan, whose company has real estate investments across Asia through its Hongkong Land unit.

Whether US-domiciled companies will be allowed to operate globally with the same degree of stability and certainty over the next decade is “a highly, highly uncertain risk that no one can underwrite,” he said.

President Donald Trump has been pushing AI investment in a race with China, even as some AI companies call for slower development and a public backlash over data centres emerges. China remains Asia’s biggest market for data centres, while outside the mainland, Western cloud providers account for about 70% of hyperscaler demand and Chinese players about 30%, according to a McKinsey report in June.

Pan’s remarks come as Firmus Grid Ltd abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings, after the Nvidia Corp-backed data centre company failed to lure global investors who have grown increasingly skittish over frothy AI valuations. Much of Firmus’ valuation was based on the company successfully building a pipeline of data centres across Asia serving customers such as Meta Platforms Inc and OpenAI.

The uncertainty extends beyond data centres to the broader AI investment boom. Despite the flood of capital into the sector, Jim Coulter, executive chairman of TPG Inc, cautioned that investors should resist assuming today’s winners and business models are already clear, saying the three most important words in AI are “I don’t know.”

Speaking on the same panel, Coulter likened investing in AI to the chaos of playing pinball, with more traditional investment akin to the repetition of 10-pin bowling.

“We have a number of themes that are very long-term themes that we’re still bowling,” he said. “But over the other side of the bowling alley, we’re playing pinball in AI because you have to shorten your cycle.”

stories.title: DayOne in early talks with banks for potential US$500 mil bond
stories.summary: DayOne Data Centers, the Singapore-based operator formerly known as GDS International, has held preliminary talks with banks for several weeks about a potential US$500 million bond offering. The fundraising effort comes as the company seeks capital to meet accelerating demand for AI infrastructure across the region.
stories.why_it_matters: A successful bond sale would give DayOne additional firepower to execute its APAC buildout while testing debt-market appetite for pure-play regional data center credits, setting a pricing benchmark for other operators contemplating similar raises.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Oct 9): DayOne Data Centers Ltd has been in preliminary talks for weeks with banks about a potential US$500 million (RM2.04 billion) bond offering, according to people familiar with the matter, as the Singapore-based company ramps up fundraising amid growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

The firm intends to push on with the discussions even after one of its project partners, Nvidia Corp-backed Firmus Grid Ltd, dropped an initial public offering plan in Australia this week, the people said, who asked not to be identified discussing private information.

Proceeds from the planned bond sale would be used for project financing, the people said. There were no details on which project or projects the money would be for. Citigroup Inc is the lead arranger for the deal and the data centre operator could go to the market as early as next year, the people said.

Representatives for DayOne and Citigroup declined to comment.

DayOne joins an increasing number of companies that are part of the broad AI buildout with plans to tap the debt market, banking on surging demand. But the failure of Firmus’ share sale attempt, in what would have been one of Australia’s largest IPOs, shows how global investors are starting to push back against what they see are frothy AI valuations.

The proceeds from Firmus’ listing would have funded purchases of graphics processing units for its first data centre project in Batam, Indonesia, that it’s developing with DayOne as part of an eight-year partnership with Nvidia.

DayOne filed for a US IPO earlier this week and has been considering to raise around US$5 billion.

AI-related data centre spending could reach US$2.9 trillion between 2025 and 2028, with around half requiring external financing, which is driving debt issuance, according to Morgan Stanley.

If DayOne taps the bond market, it would be among the first data centre firms in Asia Pacific to do so and would help others in the business to draw on larger pools of capital beyond bank financing.

Ahead of its planned bond offering, DayOne has closed half of a US$7 billion-equivalent loan — one of the largest AI-linked borrowings in Asia — with more than 30 lenders participating. The upsized part of the loan, valued at US$3.7 billion-equivalent, was split into a RM5.5 billion tranche and a US$2.4 billion portion.

DayOne has also been seeking a HK$1.86 billion (US$237 million or RM970 million) loan for a Hong Kong data centre. In August, the company obtained a four-year S$530 million (US$414 million or RM1.69 billion) to develop its first buildout in Singapore.

Other companies in the region have been aggressively raising money from the debt market to fund their AI ambitions. Billionaire Masayoshi Son’s SoftBank Group Corp last month raised the equivalent of US$11.1 billion in one of the largest corporate junk-bond offerings on record.

Once an international affiliate of Chinese data centre operator GDS Holdings Ltd, DayOne was previously known as GDS International before rebranding last year. It has brought in international investors, including SoftBank Vision Fund, Coatue Management and Ken Griffin and closed a US$4.5 billion Series C funding round in June.

Apart from Indonesia, the company is operating or developing data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Japan, Hong Kong, Thailand and Finland, according to the company’s website.

stories.title: Firmus investor Maas falls after AI data centre operator pulls blockbuster IPO plan
stories.summary: Shares of Maas Group closed more than 6% lower after Nvidia-backed Firmus abandoned its US$5 billion IPO plan. The selloff reflects investor concern over the carrying value of Maas's stake in the data center operator and its contractual exposure to the company.
stories.why_it_matters: Firmus's pulled float has immediate collateral damage beyond its own cap table: listed investors like Maas now face mark-to-market questions on private AI infrastructure holdings, a dynamic that could ripple across other public companies carrying similar stakes.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
BENGALURU (Oct 9): Maas Group's shares closed more than 6% lower on Friday after Nvidia-backed Firmus scrapped its US$5 billion IPO plan, raising concerns over the value of Maas' stake in the data centre operator and contract exposure.

The scrapped listing removed a potential public market benchmark and liquidity pathway for Maas' 3.2% stake in Firmus, while drawing investor scrutiny to JLE Group, the Australian construction services provider's electrical infrastructure unit.

"The real risk is correlation. If Firmus' funding falters, both MGH's investment and JLE's order book could come under pressure," said Hersh Oberoi, global research director at Balfour Capital Group.

The stock fell as much as 10.7% to a five-month low after trading resumed from a halt pending an update on Firmus' initial public offering and related contracts.

Oberoi said the repricing looked broadly reasonable because investors were losing an expected valuation uplift rather than facing an immediate cash hit, adding that the stake should be judged against its last private funding round, adjusted for illiquidity.

Firmus withdrew its listing application on Friday, saying market volatility and conditions would not fairly reflect its business strength and long-term growth prospects.

JLE is delivering modular Power Cubes and related electrical work under orders worth about A$1.1 billion (US$768.13 million) across fiscal 2026 and 2027.

Maas said it had received A$373 million in payments and expected the work to be completed by the end of 2027.

Maas shares slumped 22.4% on Thursday after reports that Firmus was reconsidering the offer. The stock has now shed 32% over the past week, wiping nearly A$788 million from its market value.

Firmus had planned to price its shares at A$11 each, valuing the company's equity at about A$30.6 billion, nearly triple its A$10.5 billion valuation from an August funding round.

The withdrawn float, which would have been Australia's second-largest IPO on record, underscores investor caution towards highly valued AI infrastructure firms with aggressive expansion plans and significant funding requirements.

stories.title: Unisem Plans RM396 Million Second-Phase Expansion of Gopeng Plant for AI and Data Center Chip Packaging
stories.summary: Unisem (M) Bhd (KL:UNISEM) and its subsidiary plan to invest RM396 million to expand its semiconductor manufacturing plant in Gopeng, Perak, as the group seeks to capture growing demand for advanced chip packaging used in artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres..

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 9): Unisem (M) Bhd (KL:UNISEM) and its subsidiary plan to invest RM396 million to expand its semiconductor manufacturing plant in Gopeng, Perak, as the group seeks to capture growing demand for advanced chip packaging used in artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres.

The semiconductor assembly and test services provider said the second phase of expansion will increase its manufacturing capacity for wafer bumping and post-bump services, which are used in preparing semiconductor chips for advanced packaging.

In a filing with Bursa Malaysia on Friday, Unisem said the expansion involves constructing a new production facility with a built-up area of approximately 40,000 sq m, at an estimated cost of RM196 million.

Half of the facility will be leased to its wholly owned subsidiary, Unisem Advanced Technologies Sdn Bhd, to expand wafer-bumping operations, an advanced semiconductor packaging process.

The necessary equipment and facility preparation works are expected to cost another RM200 million, bringing the total investment to RM396 million.

Unisem said the expansion is aimed at meeting growing customer demand, particularly for advanced packaging applications in AI, data centres and high-performance computing.

The project will be funded through a combination of internally generated funds and bank borrowings, although the proportions have yet to be determined.

The group said the expansion is not expected to materially affect its earnings for the current financial year but should contribute positively once completed and operational.

The latest expansion follows Unisem's earlier investment in its Gopeng facility, which began construction in March 2022. The first phase was initially estimated to cost RM300 million and was designed to double the production capacity of its existing operations in Ipoh.

In April this year, Unisem chairman and group managing director John Chia Sin Tet told *The Edge* that the group had invested RM600 million in its Gopeng plant as part of nearly RM1 billion in capital expenditure over three years.

More recently, CIMB Securities said in a September research note that Gopeng Phase 2 could drive Unisem's next leg of growth, with the expansion expected to support additional wafer-bumping and advanced packaging capacity.

At the midday break on Friday, Unisem shares were up eight sen or 1.9% at RM4.36, giving the group a market capitalisation of RM7.48 billion.

stories.title: Singapore passes Digital Infrastructure Bill for data centres, cloud
stories.summary: Singapore's Parliament has passed the Digital Infrastructure Bill, creating new licensing regimes for data centers and cloud service providers operating in the city-state. The legislation is designed to strengthen the foundations of the digital economy while imposing environmental sustainability requirements on data center operations.
stories.why_it_matters: Operators and cloud providers in Singapore now face formal licensing and compliance obligations, including sustainability mandates, that could raise the cost of doing business but also provide regulatory certainty in a market that has long balanced growth against tight energy and land constraints.
stories.content:
Singapore's Parliament has passed the Digital Infrastructure Bill, introducing two new licensing regimes. The new law aims to strengthen the foundations of Singapore's digital economy and provide regulatory clarity.It also seeks to ensure the environmental sustainability of data centre operations. The bill was initially tabled in Parliament for its First Reading in September.The new law mandates licensing for data centres with a critical IT load of at least 3 megawatts (MW). Major co-location and cloud data centres with a critical IT load of at least 10MW also fall under this requirement.Additionally, major cloud service providers whose Infrastructure-as-a-Service and Platform-as-a-Service services generate at least S$100 million (US$78.2 million) in average annual revenue from users in Singapore over the past three years are included.Major data centres will be required to implement processes ensuring the physical and cybersecurity of their services. They must also establish business continuity and disaster recovery plans.The Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) must be notified of prescribed cybersecurity incidents or service disruptions. Singapore currently operates more than 1.6GW of existing data centre capacity across 70 facilities, which includes 200MW of new capacity awarded to four operators in August.

- Policy, Land & Power
- 1 min Read

# Singapore passes Digital Infrastructure Bill for data centres, cloud

Singapore's Parliament has passed the Digital Infrastructure Bill, introducing new licensing regimes for data centres and cloud service providers. This legislation aims to enhance the digital economy's foundation and ensure environmental sustainability in data centre operations.

- Published On Oct 09, 2026 at 04:35 PM IST

## Highlights

- Singapore's Parliament passed the Digital Infrastructure Bill introducing new licensing regimes.
- Data centres with 3MW IT load and cloud providers with S$100 million revenue require licenses.
- The law mandates cybersecurity, business continuity, and environmental sustainability for major DCs.
- IMDA must be notified of cybersecurity incidents and service disruptions by licensed entities.

stories.title: AirTrunk secures US$1.21 billion green loan for Tokyo data center
stories.summary: AirTrunk has secured a ¥191.6 billion (US$1.21 billion) green loan to refinance existing debt and fund its TOK1 hyperscale data center in eastern Tokyo. The financing will support expansion of the campus as demand for AI and cloud capacity in Japan continues to climb.
stories.why_it_matters: One of the largest green financings in Japan's data center sector, the deal shows lenders remain willing to deploy billion-dollar tickets for credible hyperscale operators even as broader credit conditions tighten, and it underscores how sustainability-linked structures are becoming the default funding route for APAC data center growth.
stories.content:
AirTrunk, a hyperscale data center specialist, secured a ¥191.6 billion (US$1.21 billion) green loan to refinance existing debt and fund further development of its TOK1 hyperscale data center campus in eastern Tokyo.The expansion aims to meet growing demand for computing capacity driven by artificial intelligence and cloud services. The loan will fund capital expenditures for additional phases of TOK1, which can ultimately expand to over 300 MW.AirTrunk recently began constructing an expansion that will add more than 100 MW of IT capacity to the campus. This is to meet near-term customer demand, according to a press release.Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp. (SMBC), MUFG, Crédit Agricole CIB, and Société Générale acted as global coordinators for the financing. Twelve banks participated as mandated lead arrangers and bookrunners.Robin Khuda, founder and CEO of AirTrunk, stated that Japan is a critical market for cloud and AI. He noted that this financing accelerates the expansion of TOK1 to deliver needed capacity.Masato Hori, AirTrunk associate vice president, treasury Japan, called this the largest data center financing ever completed in Japan. He cited the deep collaboration between AirTrunk and its banking partners.The financing is structured under AirTrunk’s Green Financing Framework and is tied to the company's energy efficiency standards. Margin incentives from the loan will be directed to AirTrunk’s Social Impact Fund in Japan.AirTrunk's total investment in Japan has exceeded ¥1.2 trillion (US$8 billion) across existing and planned projects. Its four Japanese campuses, TOK1, TOK2, OSK1, and OSK2, are expected to provide about 530 MW of total capacity when fully built.

- Investments & Deals
- 1 min Read

# AirTrunk secures US$1.21 billion green loan for Tokyo data center

AirTrunk secured a ¥191.6 billion (US$1.21 billion) green loan to refinance debt and fund its TOK1 hyperscale data center in eastern Tokyo. This financing supports the expansion of the campus to meet increasing demand for AI and cloud services.

- Published On Oct 09, 2026 at 04:25 PM IST

## Highlights

- AirTrunk secured a US$1.21 billion green loan for its TOK1 data center in Tokyo.
- The financing will fund additional phases of the TOK1 campus, expanding it to over 300 MW.
- The expansion addresses rising demand for AI and cloud services in Japan.
- A consortium of 12 banks, including SMBC and MUFG, participated in the green loan.

stories.title: SoftBank, Grab, PETROS ink deal to explore AI infrastructure in Sarawak, Malaysia
stories.summary: SoftBank Group, Grab Holdings, and Sarawak's state-owned energy firm PETROS have signed a framework agreement to explore building an AI and digital infrastructure platform in the Malaysian state of Sarawak. The pact brings together a global tech investor, Southeast Asia's leading superapp, and the state's energy utility to assess development opportunities.
stories.why_it_matters: If the exploration advances, Sarawak could emerge as a new AI infrastructure hub leveraging its abundant hydropower, diversifying Malaysia's data center map beyond Johor and Selangor and giving both SoftBank and Grab a foothold in sovereign-scale compute capacity.
stories.content:
Investment firm SoftBank Group Corp., Southeast Asian superapp Grab Holdings Limited and Sarawak’s state-owned energy firm Petroleum Sarawak Berhad (“PETROS”) yesterday signed a Framework Agreement to explore the development of an artificial intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure platform in Sarawak, Malaysia, according to the firms’ joint statement yesterday.

Under the Framework Agreement, the three parties will collaborate to develop a roadmap for the phased development of the project as well as explore opportunities across the wider AI value chain, including AI compute and services, advanced technologies, robotics, local workforce and community development.

SoftBank will contribute its global technology and AI ecosystem, with expertise spanning AI infrastructure, advanced computing, semiconductors and physical AI.

Grab will contribute its Southeast Asian digital ecosystem and extensive regional customer and partner networks while PETROS will bring its experience in harnessing Sarawak’s energy resources to drive economic development. Through PETROS’ Sarawak Gas Roadmap and as Master Developer of the Kuching Low-Carbon Hub (KLCH), PETROS has vast experience in developing energy supply solutions and enabling infrastructure, facilitating local engagement, and strengthening local participation and value creation across Sarawak’s supply chain.

Sarawak is seen as having great potential in becoming a destination for AI infrastructure and high-value technology industries.

The agreement was signed by Masayoshi Son, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of SoftBank Group Corp.; Anthony Tan, Group Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Grab; and Dato Janin Girie, Group Chief Executive Officer of PETROS.

stories.title: Water constraints in Selangor could slow down data center construction in 2027
stories.summary: A research house has warned that new data center investment and construction in Selangor could slow in 2027 due to water supply constraints. Because water availability is assessed at the pre-investment stage, limited supply headroom over 2027-2029 may delay approvals for water-intensive projects, producing a temporary moderation in new data center development.
stories.why_it_matters: Water, long overshadowed by power as the gating utility, is emerging as a binding constraint in Malaysia's hottest data center corridor, which could redirect new projects toward Johor or other states and force operators to adopt less water-intensive cooling designs to keep pipelines moving.
stories.content:
New data center investment and construction could slow down in 2027 in Selangor, Malaysia due to water constraints, a research house said in a note yesterday.

“As water supply is assessed at the pre-investment stage, limited headroom over 2027–2029 may slow approvals of new water-intensive projects, potentially leading to a temporary moderation in new data centre construction awards in 2027,” BIMB Securities Research said.

As current construction of data centers takes about 18 -24 months for completion, BIMB expects new award activity to pick up again from 2028 due to the completion of Langat 2 Phase 2 water treatment and distribution system, in 2030.

Selangor state water utility, Air Selangor has a planned 2,360 million litres per day (MLD) water treatment plant (WTP) pipeline which could expand capacity by about 37 per cent through 2031. However, this could only support organic growth and projected data center water requirements of 632 MLD, resulting in tight near-term supply. The National Water Services Commission (SPAN) stipulates a 15 per cent reserve margin for water supply in the state.

The earliest completion of a WTP in the state is the Rasau WTP Stage 1 with 700 MLD capacity which is expected to go onstream in 2027. But BIMB noted that this new capacity will be absorbed by organic growth demand which averages about 3 per cent per year.

Despite the near-term tight headroom, the research house said the completion of Langat 2 Phase 2 (760 MLD) in 2030 and Rasau Stage 2 (700 MLD) in 2031, will lift data center headroom to 523 MLD in 2030 and 931 MLD in 2031 respectively.

In the long-term, continuing investment in WTP construction and pipeline replacements will ensure demand can be accommodated while near-term constraints can be mitigated by lower-water cooling designs, reclaimed water supply, or a shift to other states such as Johor, BIMB said.

stories.title: Tech stocks in Asia struggle on AI spending worries, elevated yields
stories.summary: Investors are weighing a massive round of fundraising that appears to be on the way
stories.content:
Investors are weighing a massive round of fundraising that appears to be on the way

[SINGAPORE] Asian stocks slipped on Friday (Oct 9) and were poised for a second straight weekly drop as investors fretted about elevated energy prices, bond market ructions and the huge sums needed to fund AI investment.

Brent crude futures were at US$103.70 per barrel in Asian hours after surging more than 4 per cent in the previous session on concerns over the war in the Middle East that has fanned inflation worries and led to higher rates across the globe.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November’s US midterm elections, although traders remained sceptical of any progress being made to end the war.

“The big question for markets is whether Trump sticks to his word if Iranian attacks intensify,” said Nick Twidale, chief market strategist at ATFX Global.

“Any indication that the White House is reconsidering military action could see oil prices spike sharply higher, particularly with tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz already under significant pressure.”

In stocks, MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was down 0.16 per cent, set for an over 1 per cent drop for the week. Markets in South Korea and Taiwan were closed for a holiday. Japan’s Nikkei fell more than 1 per cent.

Tech stocks led Wall Street’s main indexes lower overnight after a report that OpenAI’s annualised revenue was US$20 billion less than the company previously signalled hit sentiment.

“It has been a sea of red across technology, AI infrastructure and semiconductors, with the OpenAI headlines seemingly providing the catalyst for investors to take some exposure off the table,” said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone.

“For now, though, the price action suggests investors are becoming more selective about where they want exposure and, importantly, what price they are prepared to pay for future growth,” he said in a note.

## Bond binge for AI

Investors were also weighing a massive round of fundraising that appears to be on the way, with SpaceX, Broadcom and Oracle all expected to raise billions to buy high-end AI chips.

Australia’s Firmus, a data centre operator backed by Nvidia, shelved its US$5 billion initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, and said it would opt for a private fundraising round instead.

A toxic mix of higher energy costs, expectations of central bank interest rate hikes and concerns over rising government debts have fuelled a months-long global bond sell-off, pushing borrowing costs to multi-decade highs.

“With long-term yields back around multi-decade highs, investors no longer have the luxury of valuing AI growth in a low-cost-of-capital world,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo.

Chanana said higher sovereign yields and now rising corporate issuance to fund AI infrastructure mean capital is becoming “both more expensive and more selective, which puts balance sheets and the quality of future earnings firmly in focus.”

## Focus remains on France

France has been hit particularly hard as investors scrutinise its debt load, budget deficit and political outlook ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

“With the two rounds of the presidential elections only in April and May next year, French bond spreads are still looking at more than half a year of higher volatility and continued spread elevation,” ING analysts said in a note.

US Treasury markets have been calmer as solid auctions this week helped the mood somewhat. The benchmark 10-year yield was steady at 5.226 per cent but was not far from the 24-year high it hit on Wednesday.

“It does not mean the bond market sell-off is over, but it does at least put it on pause, at least just for now,” ING analysts said.

In currencies, the US dollar stood tall as the euro was set for a fifth straight week in the red. It last fetched US$1.122, straddling the 17-month low it touched earlier this week on French debt worries. REUTERS

stories.title: Neocloud Firmus cancels IPO, blames market volatility
stories.summary: Australian neocloud operator Firmus has withdrawn its planned IPO, citing volatile market conditions as the reason for pulling the offering. The decision marks an abrupt reversal for the Nvidia-backed company, which had been positioning the listing as one of the year's marquee AI infrastructure floats.
stories.why_it_matters: The cancellation signals that public-market appetite for AI infrastructure plays is cooling despite surging demand for compute, and it will force Firmus to seek alternative funding for its data center buildout while raising valuation questions for listed peers and shareholders with exposure to the company.
stories.content:
Australian AI cloud firm Firmus has backed out of a planned IPO, blaming volatile market conditions.

The company, which has signed deals to provide data center space for Meta and OpenAI, was due to IPO on October 23, but has now changed its plans.

It had been hoped the listing would raise $5 billion, making it one of the largest in Australian Stock Exchange history. However, as reported by *DCD* on Wednesday, the company had reduced its initial share price from AU$11 ($7.65) to AU$9 ($6.26) due to lack of interest from investors at home and abroad.

## Firmus IPO not in firm's "best interests"

In a statement shared with CNBC, Firmus said the terms of the IPO did not match the strength of the company’s proposition and its outlook for growth.

“The board therefore concluded that proceeding with the offer was not in the best interests of the company and its shareholders," the Firmus statement said. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options.”

It caps a bad week for Firmus, after it was reported it had pulled the plug on its collaboration with CDC Data Centres, dubbed Project Southgate, that could have seen 1.6GW of capacity built in Australia. Only 43MW was delivered under the agreement, though Firmus is seemingly still going ahead with the build-out, but without CDC.

In August, the company raised $2bn from backers including Nvidia and Blackstone, following a previous $505m equity investment round in April. The August round gave Firmus a post-money valuation of more than $10.5 billion.

It has signed agreements with Meta and OpenAI to provide data center capacity in Indonesia and Malaysia.

## Are the public markets shying away from backing AI data center firms?

News of the IPO being canceled will call into question the appetite of the public markets to bet on the future growth of neocloud companies like Firmus, which are planning massive AI data center build-outs but have little track record of being able to deliver infrastructure at scale.

It may also set nerves jangling at other AI cloud firms, such UK-based Nscale and US firm Lambda, which are planning listings of their own in the coming months.

Neil Osnato, founder of infrastructure advisory firm Persistence Analytics Group, said he does not believe the problems experienced by Firmus are "evidence that AI infrastructure demand is unreal," but that "capital markets are beginning to distinguish more sharply between future demand narratives and demonstrated execution."

Osnato said: "The key distinction is that market enthusiasm, customer agreements, announced capacity and delivered operating infrastructure are not the same evidentiary state.

"In Firmus’s case, the contrast is especially visible: 1.6GW was contemplated under Project Southgate, while only roughly 43MW was actually delivered under that collaboration."

He added that, in future, companies like Firmus will have to provide evidence they can deliver on their commitments, not just raise funding and attract customers, if they are to appeal to investors on the public markets.

"That distinction becomes particularly important in neocloud financing because extremely large capital commitments can be made while delivery capability, customer concentration, power availability, construction execution and future utilization remain dependent on one another," Osnato said.

stories.title: Interactive: Why the Asean Power Grid's future lies in subsea cables
stories.summary: Some of the world’s longest subsea power cables could be laid in the region, if vision can translate to action
stories.content:
Some of the world’s longest subsea power cables could be laid in the region, if vision can translate to action

South-east Asian countries have long traded electricity via land-based power cables. But achieving the Asean Power Grid (APG) – a decades-old vision to link up the bloc’s power systems – calls for a deep dive into the ocean.

Subsea interconnectors will be vital to realise the APG. These are high-voltage power cable systems laid on or under the seabed, transmitting electricity from one country to another.

## Vikings ahoy!

Today, the world’s longest subsea interconnector runs 630 km between the UK and Denmark. It is part of the Viking Link, a network of high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables that allows both countries to exchange power from sources such as offshore wind.

Source: National Grid

If the Viking Link seems massive, South-east Asia could take subsea interconnectors to a whole new scale.

The region already has several overland interconnectors, mostly used by Laos to export electricity to its neighbours – including Singapore, via Thailand and Malaysia, as part of a breakthrough APG project.

The APG envisions many more interconnectors, including those that could connect Singapore to Cambodia, Vietnam, Sarawak in East Malaysia, and the Riau Islands and Sumatra in Indonesia.

Singapore aims to import 6 gigawatts (GW) of low-carbon electricity by 2035, meeting about one-third of its energy demand then.

To obtain an import licence, companies will first need to receive conditional approval from Singapore’s energy regulator, followed by a conditional licence.

The Energy Market Authority (EMA) has thus far granted conditional approvals to projects that seek to import 6.25 GW of clean energy from destinations such as Cambodia, Vietnam and even as far away as Australia.

EMA has also granted conditional licences to six projects that could bring in 3 GW of clean energy from Indonesia.

With such projects in the works, the market for subsea power cables is “expanding steadily”, said Sandra Seah, a partner at law firm Bird & Bird with expertise in energy.

She noted that ZTT Group, a Chinese advanced manufacturing player, “has stepped up its game” with major manufacturing and research bases in the region for medium-voltage and high-voltage subsea power cables.

Cable installers – who specialise in the transportation, installation and protection of subsea power cables – “are also becoming more active in the Asean market”, said Seah.

## Ambitious leap

Realising these projects will be a big leap. The region currently only has one subsea interconnector: between Plentong in Johor, Malaysia and Singapore’s Woodlands.

Established in 1983 and upgraded in 2022, the link supports bidirectional electricity flows of up to 1 GW. It spans just 2 km, a fraction of the UK-Denmark Viking Link, according to data compiled by the International Energy Agency (IEA).

For the APG to truly take off, subsea cables would have to run much longer distances, beating even the Viking Link. For instance, an undersea interconnector from Malaysia to Vietnam could span 700 km.

One from Singapore to Sarawak may run 750 km.

And another from the city-state to Vietnam or to Cambodia may have to cross at least 1,000 km.

The APG is a “step change in ambition for the region”, said Tan Sue-Ern, head of IEA Regional Cooperation Centre.

“Several planned subsea cable projects are significantly more complex than what came before – with cables spanning long distances, crossing multiple jurisdictions, and requiring specialised vessels and expertise for cable installation and repair,” she told *The Business Times*.

### 2 km

### 630 km

### ~700 km

### ~750 km

### ~1,000 km

### >1,000 km

IEA estimated US$27 billion is needed between 2025 and 2040 to deliver the proposed pipeline of energy interconnection projects, inclusive of both overland and subsea cables.

This is more than 10 times the US$2 billion that the region invested in energy interconnectors from the 1970s to 2024, mostly for one-way power export.

## Caution: high voltage

Building these long-distance interconnectors will require HVDC cables, as well as specialised vessels to lay them. But the global market for these resources is tight.

Lam Pham, an Asia energy analyst at think tank Ember, noted that Asean still lacks manufacturing capacity for such cables within the region, and is thus “heavily dependent” on established suppliers and installation capacity from elsewhere.

“(With) Asean projects competing for the same manufacturing slots and installation capacity as Europe’s offshore wind industry, (this) is pushing up costs and creating long lead times for new projects,” he said.

## Cross-section of a HVDC subsea cable

The interactive cutaway loads as you reach this section.

Illustrative single-core extruded HVDC cable based on the Europacable reference. Layer proportions and colours are schematic.

Sources: Europacable, ZMS Cable

Assaad Razzouk, CEO of Singapore-based renewable power company Gurin Energy, called for centralised procurement of subsea power cables to mitigate supply constraints.

“Governments should give us a hand in procuring these ahead of time, so that as a region, we don’t find ourselves in five years without the ability to… build the Asean grid because the rest of the world gobbled (the cables),” he said at an industry event in August.

## Cracking the puzzle

Regulatory clarity is another key piece of the puzzle.

For subsea cable manufacturers to establish production or installation operations in Asean, they will need greater certainty around the project pipeline and government policy, Lam noted.

Seah echoed this, noting that transmission infrastructure is capital-intensive and will only be developed where there is “demonstrable demand”.

Sentiment around the APG is still cautious. In a recent survey of energy professionals, only a quarter expect significant cross-border power trading in the next decade. Over half of respondents believed that a fully integrated regional grid “will remain some way off”.

This comes amid obstacles that APG projects face. The Singapore-Indonesia projects, for instance, have run into delays over regulatory uncertainty.

Jakarta requires clean energy exporters to renew permits every five years. But this frequent renewal timeframe leads to a lack of confidence among potential investors and offtakers.

Asean member states have also not formally agreed on a single framework governing subsea cable assets under the APG, and whether ownership will be public or private, noted Seah.

## Key development to watch

The status quo could change, as Asean works on its Submarine Power Cable Development Framework.

The framework will cover four aspects around the laying and maintenance of subsea power cables: legal and regulatory, technical, commercial, and governance issues.

In October last year, Asean’s energy ministers reaffirmed the importance of the framework during their annual meeting, calling for “sustained and accelerated progress”.

The completion of this framework will be a key milestone to watch out for.

Asean's diversity of technical standards and political priorities will need to be taken into consideration, said Seah, noting that the region currently uses more than 20 grid codes.

As she put it, the process will take “time and trust”.

**Sources:** Rystad Energy, International Energy Agency, Sustainable Energy Association of Singapore, data compiled by BT

**Graphic:** Ho Yan Hao, Nurulshazanani Idris, BT (with AI assistance)

stories.title: FedEx study sees Asia Pacific semiconductor expansion
stories.summary: Geopolitical risks are prompting chipmakers to spread production across Asia Pacific, with 35% planning expansion into new regional markets.
stories.content:
FedEx has published a report on semiconductor and digital infrastructure supply chains in Asia Pacific. The study found that 35% of surveyed semiconductor companies expect to expand manufacturing into additional markets across the region.

Produced with Frost & Sullivan, the report examines how demand from artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, electric vehicles and advanced communications technology is reshaping semiconductor production and logistics in Asia Pacific. The region accounts for about 58% of global semiconductor industry revenue, it said.

Survey data points to continued regional expansion. Another 25% of respondents said they plan to increase or diversify sourcing within Asia Pacific or globally over the next three years, while 30% identified geopolitical disruption as the biggest challenge to growth.

FedEx surveyed 478 semiconductor industry participants from companies, industry associations and research institutes in Asia Pacific, Europe and North America. Responses were collected in Taipei and covered growth expectations, supply chain strategy, expansion challenges and logistics needs.

### AI demand

The findings place artificial intelligence and high-performance computing at the centre of semiconductor demand growth. The report also highlights continued demand from electric vehicles, 5G, the internet of things, consumer electronics, medical devices and industrial automation.

Beyond chips, the study examines the equipment needed to support the AI economy, including servers, networking equipment, cooling systems and power solutions. These products often pass through several manufacturing, assembly and testing hubs before deployment, adding complexity to cross-border supply chains.

That complexity is shaping logistics choices. According to the survey, 44% of respondents said faster international shipping would be the most important factor when choosing logistics and supply chain partners over the next three years.

### Regional roles

The report describes Asia Pacific as a network of specialised semiconductor hubs rather than a single manufacturing centre. It identifies China as a major materials supplier, consumer market and growing fabrication base, while Taiwan is described as the leading market for advanced semiconductor manufacturing and as accounting for roughly 60% of global foundry output.

South Korea is identified as a leading producer of memory chips and advanced fabrication, while Japan is highlighted for equipment, materials and specialist manufacturing inputs. Southeast Asia, meanwhile, is presented as an important base for assembly, packaging and testing operations.

As a result, design, fabrication, packaging, testing and deployment often take place across multiple countries before a finished product reaches the market. The report says this structure is creating a more interconnected supply chain as companies work to meet rising demand across industries.

### Resilience focus

The survey suggests companies are putting greater emphasis on resilience alongside efficiency. Geopolitical uncertainty, regulation and customs complexity are among the pressures affecting operations, pushing businesses to diversify manufacturing locations and suppliers.

According to the findings, traditional just-in-time models are being supplemented by inventory buffers and broader sourcing strategies. That shift has increased the importance of logistics networks that can handle time-sensitive, high-value shipments across multiple jurisdictions.

Nearly four in five respondents identified Taiwan, Southeast Asia, Greater China and Japan as the markets expected to record the largest increase in semiconductor demand over the next three years. The report said this outlook reflects both the strength of established production hubs and the broader regionalisation of supply chains.

FedEx linked the findings to recent changes in its own network, including daily direct flights between Taiwan and South Korea and the expansion of its Taoyuan transhipment centre in Taiwan. It said the changes were intended to handle rising volumes of semiconductor and advanced technology shipments across the region.

"The next decade of innovation will be shaped not only by advances in semiconductors, but by the strength and resilience of the supply chains that power AI and digital infrastructure," said Salil Chari, President, Asia Pacific, FedEx.

"As investment in AI infrastructure accelerates, businesses are managing increasingly complex supply chains spanning semiconductors, servers, networking equipment, cooling systems and advanced technology components across multiple markets. Resilience, visibility and agility have become strategic advantages. FedEx is helping customers connect these critical supply chains through our extensive APAC network, global reach and specialized logistics capabilities, enabling innovation to move faster from factory floor to data center," said Chari.

stories.title: Stocks to watch: Frasers Property, StarHub, NTT DC Reit
stories.summary: [SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Oct 9):
stories.content:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Oct 9):

Frasers Property : The CEO of Frasers Hospitality Eu Chin Fen will be stepping down, effective Jan 1, 2027. This follows the privatisation of Frasers Hospitality Trust and its portfolio optimisation. Frasers Hospitality’s leadership structure “will be strategically segmented, aligning with group resources, and reporting into senior group leadership”. Its chief operating officer Chew Hang Song will report to the group CEO. The counter closed at S$0.955 on Thursday, down S$0.01 or 1 per cent.

StarHub : The telco said it will acquire MyRepublic’s mobile business by Apr 30, 2027. The value of the transaction is not fixed, but is dependent on the total 4G and 5G MyRepublic mobile subscribers, average revenue per user of active 4G and 5G subscribers, as well as subscriber lifetime. StarHub will also pay additional cash amounts when specific subscriber migration milestones are met. Shares of StarHub ended at S$1.10 on Thursday, S$0.02 or 1.8 per cent lower.

NTT DC Reit : The real estate investment trust’s (Reit) manager is proposing changes to its management fee structure, that it expects will better align with the interests of the unitholders of the Reit. It is looking to link its performance fee directly to year-on-year growth in the distribution per unit. Units of NTT DC Reit ended 0.5 per cent or US$0.005 lower at US$0.935 on Thursday.
